title: Containers
scopeHtml: Scope: namespaces, cgroups, how Docker works, CPU throttling, OOM in containers and debugging.

notes.title: A container is a process with blinders
notes.html:
A container is not a small virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process (or group of processes) that the kernel has been told to show a limited view of the system, and to limit in resource use. There is no guest kernel: every container on a host shares the host's kernel.

Two kernel features do all the work:

  • Namespaces limit what a process can see (its own process list, network, mounts, hostname, users).
  • cgroups (control groups) limit what a process can use (CPU, memory, I/O, number of processes).
  • Plus a layered file system (overlayfs) for the image, capabilities, seccomp and LSMs (AppArmor/SELinux) for restricting what it may do.

Worked example. Start a container and look at it from the host:

$ docker run -d --name web --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 nginx
$ docker top web
UID  PID   PPID  CMD
root 18211 18190 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
$ ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p 18211          # on the HOST it is just a process
  PID  PPID CMD
18211 18190 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
$ docker exec web ps aux | head -2     # INSIDE it thinks it is PID 1
PID USER  COMMAND
  1 root  nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;

Same process: host PID 18211, container PID 1. That one fact explains most of Docker.

VM vs container.

VM Container
Kernel Own guest kernel on virtual hardware Host kernel, shared
Start time Seconds to minutes Milliseconds to ~1 s
Overhead GB of RAM per guest MBs
Isolation Strong (hypervisor boundary) Weaker (kernel bug or misconfig can escape)
Density Tens per host Hundreds to thousands per host

Industry examples. Google ran containers on cgroups for years before Docker (Borg); Kubernetes descends from that. AWS Lambda and Fargate use Firecracker microVMs because multi-tenant strangers need VM-grade isolation. gVisor and Kata Containers add a user-space kernel or a light VM for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. Flats in one building: separate front doors and rooms (namespaces), a water and electricity meter each (cgroups), but one shared foundation (the kernel). A VM is a separate house.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying containers have their own kernel. They do not; uname -r inside equals the host's.
  • Treating containers as a security boundary equal to VMs for untrusted code.

notes.title: Namespaces
notes.html:
A namespace wraps a global system resource so that processes inside see their own private instance. Each is created with a flag to clone(), unshare() or setns().

Namespace Flag Isolates Effect
PID CLONE_NEWPID Process IDs First process is PID 1; cannot see host processes
NET CLONE_NEWNET Interfaces, routes, iptables, ports Own eth0, own port 80
MNT CLONE_NEWNS Mount points Own root file system view
UTS CLONE_NEWUTS Hostname Container name as hostname
IPC CLONE_NEWIPC SysV IPC, POSIX queues Private shared memory
USER CLONE_NEWUSER UID/GID mapping Root inside = unprivileged outside
CGROUP CLONE_NEWCGROUP cgroup root view Hides host cgroup paths
TIME CLONE_NEWTIME Boot/monotonic clock offset Rarely used 
$ sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts bash       # make your own mini-container
# hostname demo; ps aux
USER  PID COMMAND
root    1 bash
root    9 ps aux
$ ls -l /proc/18211/ns          # every process's namespace handles
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 net -> 'net:[4026532601]'
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 pid -> 'pid:[4026532599]'
$ sudo nsenter -t 18211 -n ss -ltn    # enter just its network namespace from the host
LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80

nsenter is the tool to debug a container whose image has no tools: run the host's ss, tcpdump, strace inside its namespaces.

Container networking. Docker creates a veth pair (a virtual cable): one end inside the container's net namespace as eth0, the other plugged into a bridge (docker0) on the host. NAT (iptables/nftables) sends outbound traffic out and -p 8080:80 rewrites inbound packets (DNAT). In Kubernetes, all containers of a pod share one network namespace (that is why they share localhost), and a CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, AWS VPC CNI) wires pods.

PID 1 matters. In a PID namespace the first process is init: it ignores signals it has no handler for (so docker stop's SIGTERM is ignored by a naive app, and Docker kills it after 10 s with SIGKILL), and it must reap orphaned zombies. Use docker run --init (tini) or write signal handlers.

User namespaces. Map container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID such as 100000. Even if the process escapes, it is nobody on the host. Rootless Podman and Docker rootless use it.

Decision gravity. Running as non-root with a user namespace is cheap to adopt early and painful to retrofit when files and volumes assume UID 0. Prefer it from day one.

Industry examples. Kubernetes shares network, IPC and UTS namespaces inside a pod, but each container has its own mount and PID namespace unless shareProcessNamespace: true is set (useful for debug sidecars).

Everyday analogy. Hotel rooms: each guest has their own phone line, room numbers and bathroom (private views) but the same building.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up what namespaces do (visibility) and what cgroups do (limits).
  • Expecting a SIGTERM handler to work when the app is not PID 1 behind a shell script (CMD ./start.sh swallows signals; use exec).
  • Forgetting that the host can always see everything in the container.

notes.title: cgroups
notes.html:
Control groups account and limit resource use for a set of processes. They form a tree under /sys/fs/cgroup; each directory is a group; writing a PID into cgroup.procs moves a process in; child groups inherit and split the parent's limits. Controllers: cpu, memory, io, pids, cpuset, hugetlb, rdma.

Linux has v1 (one hierarchy per controller) and v2 (unified hierarchy, default in current distros, Docker 20.10+, Kubernetes 1.25+ GA).

$ cat /proc/18211/cgroup
0::/system.slice/docker-3f9a....scope
$ cd /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-3f9a....scope
$ cat memory.max cpu.max pids.max
536870912          # 512 MiB
150000 100000      # quota 150 ms per 100 ms period = 1.5 CPUs
max
$ cat memory.current
218103808
$ cat memory.events
low 0
high 0
max 12
oom 1
oom_kill 1         # this group has had an OOM kill

Key files (v2): memory.max (hard limit), memory.high (throttle point), memory.swap.max, cpu.max, cpu.weight (relative share, default 100), cpu.stat, io.max, pids.max, cpuset.cpus.

Two styles of limit:

  • Weights (shares): only matter under contention. cpu.weight 200 vs 100 gives 2:1 when both are busy; an idle CPU is free for anyone. Kubernetes requests map to this.
  • Hard caps: enforced always. cpu.max quota and memory.max. Kubernetes limits map to these.

Worked example (Kubernetes mapping).

resources:
  requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduling + cpu.weight (~ 500m -> weight)
  limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "512Mi" }   # cpu.max = 100000/100000, memory.max = 512Mi

The scheduler places the pod on a node with 500m and 256Mi free (requests). The cgroup caps it at 1 CPU and 512 MiB (limits). QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable, BestEffort (none); under node memory pressure BestEffort pods are evicted first.

Industry examples. systemd puts every service in its own cgroup (systemd-cgls, systemctl set-property nginx.service MemoryMax=1G). Google Borg, Kubernetes and Mesos all use cgroups for isolation and bin-packing.

Everyday analogy. A shared flat's utility meter with a monthly cap per tenant: the weights say who gets more when everyone is home, the hard caps say a stop-the-flow limit.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing requests are enforced limits. CPU request is a weight and scheduling hint; memory request is only used for scheduling and eviction ranking.
  • Not knowing v1 vs v2 file names (memory.limit_in_bytes vs memory.max).

notes.title: How Docker really works
notes.html:
Docker is a friendly front end over a stack of components; the Linux kernel does the real work.

  1. docker CLI sends REST calls to the dockerd daemon over /var/run/docker.sock (anyone with that socket is effectively root on the host).
  2. dockerd handles images, networks, volumes, and delegates containers to containerd (also used directly by Kubernetes via CRI).
  3. containerd manages image pulls, snapshots and container lifecycle; it starts containerd-shim per container so the container survives daemon restarts.
  4. runc (OCI reference runtime) reads the OCI bundle (config.json + root fs), calls clone with namespace flags, sets up cgroups, mounts, drops capabilities, installs seccomp, then execves your command and exits. The shim stays as the parent.

Images and layers. An image is a stack of read-only layers (tarballs of file changes, identified by SHA-256 digest) plus a config JSON. overlayfs merges them: lowerdir = read-only layers, upperdir = the container's writable layer, merged = what the process sees. Writing to a file from a lower layer triggers copy-up (copy the whole file first, then modify), so heavy writes inside the container layer are slow; use volumes.

$ docker inspect web --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.MergedDir}}'
/var/lib/docker/overlay2/9c1a.../merged
$ mount | grep overlay
overlay on /var/lib/docker/overlay2/9c1a.../merged type overlay
  (rw,lowerdir=l/AA:l/BB:l/CC,upperdir=9c1a.../diff,workdir=9c1a.../work)
$ docker history nginx | head -4       # one layer per Dockerfile instruction

Dockerfile hygiene. Layer order controls cache reuse: put rarely changing steps (OS packages, dependency install) first and source code last. Multi-stage builds keep compilers out of the final image (Java: 700 MB build image, 150 MB runtime image).

# Dockerfile: dependency layer cached until pom.xml changes
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN mvn -B package -DskipTests
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build target/app.jar /app.jar
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]

Security knobs. Default capability set is reduced (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN), default seccomp profile blocks about 40+ dangerous syscalls, --read-only root, --cap-drop ALL, --security-opt no-new-privileges. --privileged removes nearly all of it: avoid.

Volumes and state. A container's writable layer dies with it. Bind mounts and named volumes attach host directories (bypass overlayfs, good for databases).

Decision gravity. Choosing an image base (alpine/musl vs debian-slim/glibc vs distroless) is a long-lived decision: musl DNS and performance quirks, no shell for debugging in distroless (use kubectl debug ephemeral containers). Reversible via rebuild, but costs testing.

Industry examples. Kubernetes dropped dockershim (v1.24) and talks to containerd or CRI-O directly; the images stay compatible because of the OCI standards. Podman runs without a central daemon.

Everyday analogy. Docker is the shipping company's booking desk; runc is the crane that actually loads the container; the ship (kernel) carries everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Docker needs a hypervisor on Linux. It does not (Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows runs a hidden Linux VM).
  • Storing data in the container layer, then losing it on redeploy.
  • Running as root and mounting docker.sock into containers.

notes.title: CPU limits and throttling
notes.html:
A CPU limit in a container is a quota of CPU time per period, not a number of cores. With the CFS bandwidth controller, cpu.max = 150000 100000 means the group may use 150 ms of CPU time every 100 ms period (1.5 cores). Once the quota is spent, all threads in the group are paused until the next period, even if the machine is idle.

Limit 1 CPU = 100 ms quota per 100 ms period. App has 8 threads, all busy.
Period starts: 8 threads run in parallel on 8 cores -> 100 ms quota burns in 12.5 ms
Remaining 87.5 ms of the period: ALL threads frozen (throttled)
A request that needed 20 ms of CPU now takes 20 ms + up to 87.5 ms wait.

Symptom. Average CPU utilisation looks low (30%), yet p99 latency is bad. The cause is throttling, visible in:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat
usage_usec 91233018221
user_usec 80112200100
system_usec 11120818121
nr_periods 612300
nr_throttled 301220          # throttled in ~49% of periods
throttled_usec 4812001299    # total throttled time ~4,812 s
$ kubectl top pod api-7d9f   # shows 300m of 1000m, looks fine!

Prometheus: rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]). Above about 5 to 25% is worth acting on.

Why multi-threaded runtimes suffer. The JVM sizes thread pools (GC threads, ForkJoin, Netty event loops) from the number of visible cores unless it detects the cgroup. Java 10+ is container aware (-XX:ActiveProcessorCount to override); Go before 1.25 saw all host cores in GOMAXPROCS (use uber-go/automaxprocs, newer Go versions respect the quota); Node and Python workers can similarly oversubscribe. A 64-core node, a 1 CPU limit, and 64 GC threads = constant throttling.

Fixes (in order).

  1. Raise or remove the CPU limit while keeping the request (many large operators, such as Tim Hockin's well-known Kubernetes advice, set CPU requests only and let pods burst; memory limit = request).
  2. Fit thread counts to the quota (GOMAXPROCS, -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2, fewer workers).
  3. Use cpuset / Kubernetes static CPU manager policy for exclusive cores (Guaranteed pods with integer CPU).
  4. Kernel burst: cpu.max.burst (cgroup v2, kernel 5.14+) lets unused quota accumulate. Older kernels had a CFS quota accounting bug fixed in 5.4 that caused excess throttling.

Worked example. Service with limit 2 CPUs, request 2, running 16 Tomcat/Netty worker threads. Quota per 100 ms: 200 ms. A spike of 16 busy threads burns 200 ms in 12.5 ms, then 87.5 ms frozen. Request latency p99 goes from 30 ms to 130 ms. Setting limit 4 (or removing it) and capping threads at 4 cut p99 back to 35 ms and nr_throttled to near zero.

Decision gravity. CPU limit: yes for noisy multi-tenant fairness, no for latency-critical services (use requests/weights). Memory limit: always. Both are reversible with a pod rollout.

Industry examples. Public writeups (Omio, Indeed, Zalando) blamed throttling for latency spikes and chose to drop CPU limits. Google Borg uses CPU shares plus per-class limits.

Everyday analogy. A prepaid data pack renewed every 100 ms: burn it all in the first 12 ms and the line is cut until renewal, even though the network is free.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading average CPU % and concluding no CPU problem.
  • Equating cpu: 1 with one core. It is 100 ms per 100 ms spread across any cores.
  • Not telling the runtime about the limit.

notes.title: Memory limits and OOM in containers
notes.html:
A memory limit (memory.max) is a hard ceiling for all processes in the cgroup: heap, stacks, page cache, kernel memory, tmpfs. When usage reaches the limit the kernel first tries to reclaim (drop clean page cache, swap if allowed); if it cannot, the cgroup OOM killer picks a process in that group and sends SIGKILL. No chance to log or clean up; the exit status is 137 (128 + 9) and Kubernetes shows OOMKilled.

$ kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -A6 'Last State'
    Last State:   Terminated
      Reason:     OOMKilled
      Exit Code:  137
$ dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'
[Mon Nov  9 10:21:08] Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18211 (java)
   total-vm:6291456kB, anon-rss:524288kB, file-rss:12288kB, shmem-rss:0kB
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.events
oom_kill 3
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.stat | head -6
anon 497000448       # heap, stack: cannot be dropped
file 12582912        # page cache: reclaimable
kernel 9437184

What counts toward the limit. Anonymous memory (heap), page cache from files the container touches (reclaimable, but under pressure it causes slow reclaim "thrashing" before OOM), tmpfs / emptyDir: medium: Memory, kernel structures. Hence "working set" (container_memory_working_set_bytes) = usage minus inactive file cache is what Kubernetes uses for eviction decisions.

Two different OOM kinds.

  • Container OOM (cgroup): the container hit its own limit; only it is killed.
  • Node OOM / eviction: the host is out of memory; the kubelet evicts pods (Evicted, per QoS class) or the global kernel OOM killer fires, scoring by oom_score_adj (Guaranteed pods get -997, BestEffort 1000).

Language runtime pitfalls.

  • JVM: heap is only part of memory (metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers, GC structures). -Xmx = limit means certain OOM kill. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 (container aware since JDK 10; JDK 8u191+ backport). Example: limit 1 GiB, heap 700 MiB, rest 300 MiB for the other pieces.
  • Go: set GOMEMLIMIT to about 90% of the container limit (Go 1.19+) so the GC works harder before the kernel kills the process.
  • Node: --max-old-space-size below the limit.
  • Python / glibc malloc arenas: fragmentation raises RSS; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 often helps.
  • Memory leak vs just limit too low: a sawtooth that always returns to a baseline is fine; a ramp that never falls is a leak.

Worked example. A Java service has limit: 1Gi, -Xmx1g. Starting up it takes heap 600 MiB + metaspace 90 MiB + 200 threads x 1 MiB stacks + 150 MiB direct buffers = about 1.05 GiB. Under load the heap grows to 900 MiB and the pod dies with exit 137 every few hours; kubectl get pod shows restarts climbing. Fix: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65, limit 1.5Gi, and cap Netty direct memory with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m.

Swap. Kubernetes traditionally disabled swap on nodes; cgroup v2 memory.swap.max and the NodeSwap feature are now supported (check your version). With swap off, no cushion exists.

Decision gravity. Setting memory request = limit makes the pod Guaranteed-like for memory and predictable; overcommit (limit > request) risks node-level eviction. One-way for stateful data: a killed database can lose in-flight transactions, so size with headroom.

Industry examples. Common root causes in postmortems: JVM heap flags ignoring non-heap memory, tmpfs-backed emptyDir counting as memory, sidecar containers (Envoy) hitting small limits, and log buffers in memory.

Everyday analogy. A hotel room with a hard occupancy limit: the guests (heap), furniture (kernel structures) and luggage (page cache) all count; luggage can be moved out (reclaimed), but the guests are the problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit.
  • Confusing exit 137 with a crash in the app code. 137 is SIGKILL; check OOMKilled and dmesg.
  • Believing page cache does not count. It does, though it is reclaimable first.
  • Looking only at heap metrics while RSS includes much more.

notes.title: Debugging containers in production
notes.html:
You often have no shell, no tools, and a restarted pod that erased the evidence.

Workflow:

# 1. Why did it restart?
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -E 'Reason|Exit Code|Restart Count'
kubectl logs api-7d9f --previous              # logs of the crashed instance
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail

# 2. Live resource use from the container's own cgroup
kubectl exec api-7d9f -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat

# 3. Add tools without changing the image (ephemeral debug container sharing the target's namespaces)
kubectl debug -it api-7d9f --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api

# 4. From the node: enter just the network namespace and use host tools
PID=$(crictl inspect --output go-template --template '{{.info.pid}}' <container-id>)
nsenter -t $PID -n ss -tnp
nsenter -t $PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 -c 50 port 8080

Checklist for typical symptoms:

  • Restarts with 137: memory limit (see above).
  • Restarts with 143 or "Liveness probe failed": SIGTERM or probe timeout; a CPU-throttled app fails its probe; raise timeoutSeconds or the limit.
  • Latency spikes with low CPU%: nr_throttled in cpu.stat.
  • Pending pod: requests do not fit any node; kubectl describe shows Insufficient cpu.
  • Disk pressure / evictions: container logs and writable layers fill the node (ephemeral-storage limits).
  • DNS slow (5 s delays): conntrack races and ndots:5; use a node-local DNS cache.
  • Too many open files / pids.max reached: fork bomb or thread leak; check pids.current vs pids.max.

Industry examples. Netflix's Titus and Google's tooling capture cgroup stats continuously; cAdvisor (inside kubelet) exports container_* metrics that Prometheus scrapes.

Everyday analogy. Investigating a locked flat: first read the landlord's notes (orchestrator events), then the meters (cgroup), then ask the neighbours (host tools) before breaking in.

Common interview traps.

  • kubectl logs without --previous after a crash loop shows an empty new instance.
  • Judging resource problems from node-level graphs rather than per-container cgroup metrics.
  • Forgetting that exec into a distroless container fails; use an ephemeral container.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A container = Linux process + namespaces (see) + cgroups (use) + overlayfs root + capabilities/seccomp. It shares the host kernel; VMs do not.
  • Namespaces: PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP, TIME. Use nsenter and unshare to explore. Be careful with PID 1 and signals.
  • cgroups v2: memory.max, cpu.max, cpu.weight, pids.max; Kubernetes requests are scheduling hints and weights, limits are hard caps.
  • Docker stack: CLI, dockerd, containerd, runc; image layers via overlayfs with copy-up; keep data in volumes; run non-root with dropped capabilities.
  • CPU limit is a quota per 100 ms period: bursts of threads cause throttling and p99 spikes with low average CPU; watch nr_throttled; match runtime thread counts to the limit; consider requests-only for latency-critical services.
  • Memory limit is hard; OOM kill is SIGKILL, exit 137; JVM, Go, Node need limits below the container limit; page cache and tmpfs count.
  • Debug outside-in: kubectl describe/logs --previous, cgroup files, kubectl debug, nsenter.

questions.promptHtml: What is a container, and how is it different from a virtual machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common containers question. The signal is whether you know there is no guest kernel.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A container is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been told to show a limited view of the system (namespaces) and to limit in resource use (cgroups). There is no guest OS: all containers share the host kernel. A VM runs its own kernel on virtual hardware, so it is heavier but has much stronger isolation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Container = process + namespaces (what it SEES) + cgroups (what it USES)
            + overlayfs root + capabilities/seccomp/LSM (what it may DO)

You can prove it: the same nginx is PID 18211 on the host and PID 1 inside the container, and uname -r inside equals the host's.

VM Container
Kernel own guest kernel host kernel, shared
Start seconds to minutes milliseconds to ~1 s
Overhead GBs RAM per guest MBs
Isolation hypervisor boundary weaker: kernel bug or misconfig can escape
Density tens/host hundreds to thousands

Multi-tenant clouds that run strangers' code (AWS Lambda, Fargate) use Firecracker microVMs; gVisor and Kata add a user-space kernel or light VM to harden containers. On Mac/Windows, Docker Desktop silently runs a Linux VM.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Containers have their own OS". They have their own filesystem image, not a kernel.
  • Treating containers as an equal security boundary to VMs for untrusted code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a Linux container run on a Windows host kernel directly? -> No; Docker Desktop uses a Linux VM (WSL2).
  2. Why start so fast? -> It is just clone + execve of a process, no boot.
  3. When would you pick a VM? -> Strong isolation, different kernel versions or OS, regulated multi-tenancy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "lightweight VM". Senior: process plus namespaces and cgroups, shared-kernel implications for security and kernel upgrades, microVM alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team found their "isolated" containers all crashed together when a kernel bug triggered on the shared host.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between namespaces and cgroups? Give an example of each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Confusing visibility with limits is the most common mistake.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Namespaces control what a process can see: its own PIDs, network interfaces, mounts, hostname, users. cgroups control how much it can use: CPU, memory, I/O, number of processes. A PID namespace makes my process think it is PID 1; a memory cgroup makes the kernel kill it if it exceeds 512 MiB.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Namespace Isolates Effect
PID process IDs first process is PID 1
NET interfaces, routes, iptables, ports own eth0, own port 80
MNT mount points own root filesystem view
UTS hostname container name as hostname
IPC SysV IPC, queues private shared memory
USER uid/gid mapping root inside = unprivileged outside
CGROUP / TIME cgroup root / clock offsets rare

Created via clone(), unshare() and entered via setns(). You can make a mini container by hand:

sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts bash
# ps aux  -> shows bash as PID 1
ls -l /proc/18211/ns          # namespace handles of any process
sudo nsenter -t 18211 -n ss -ltn   # host's ss inside the container's net namespace

The host can always see everything in the container; namespaces are one-way blinders.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Namespaces limit memory": no, that is cgroups.
  • Forgetting that Kubernetes pod containers share net, IPC and UTS namespaces but have separate mount and PID namespaces by default.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does container networking work? -> A veth pair: one end is eth0 in the container, the other plugs into a host bridge; NAT does the rest.
  2. What does a user namespace buy? -> Root in the container maps to an unprivileged host UID; used by rootless Podman/Docker.
  3. How do you debug a container with no tools? -> nsenter from the host using the host's tools.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names them. Senior: lists namespace types, the clone flags, nsenter debugging, pod sharing and user-namespace security.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tcpdump inside a distroless pod was impossible until the team used nsenter -n from the node.

questions.contextHtml:
A service runs in Docker with CMD ./start.sh, where start.sh does some setup and then runs java -jar app.jar. During rolling deploys, each pod takes exactly 30 s to terminate in Kubernetes (the default grace period), in-flight requests are cut, and the app's shutdown hook that flushes a queue never logs "flush complete". Logs of the previous run:

10:01:05 Received SIGTERM  <- not present
(no shutdown hook output)
kubectl describe: Last State: Terminated  Reason: Error  Exit Code: 137

Red herring: someone suspects the JVM shutdown hook has a bug.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it behave like this and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds." That just waits longer for a signal that never arrives.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is PID 1 in the container? Does start.sh use exec? Is there an init like tini? Does the app log anything on SIGTERM when run manually?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Change the entrypoint so the JVM receives SIGTERM; as a quick alternative run docker run --init.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) PID 1 is the shell script and it does not forward SIGTERM to its child; (b) PID 1 has no default signal handler, so signals without a handler are ignored; (c) the hook itself is buggy (least likely since it never ran).
  4. How I'd verify: kubectl exec pod -- ps -o pid,args shows 1 /bin/sh ./start.sh and java as PID 7. docker stop takes 10 s then kills; exit code 137 means SIGKILL.
  5. Root cause: In a PID namespace PID 1 is special: signals with no handler are ignored for it, and a shell does not relay SIGTERM. After the grace period the kubelet sends SIGKILL, so the hook never runs.
  6. Fix: In start.sh end with exec java -jar app.jar so the JVM replaces the shell and becomes PID 1 (JVM handles SIGTERM), or use ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"] in exec form, or add tini (--init) to forward signals and reap zombies.
#!/bin/sh
# setup...
exec java -jar /app.jar
  1. Prevention: A deploy test that asserts the process stops in under N seconds; lint Dockerfiles for shell-form CMD; add a preStop sleep for LB drain.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the grace period as the fix; I would also not trap signals in shell scripts if exec solves it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does PID 1 also matter for zombies? -> Orphaned children get re-parented to PID 1, which must wait() for them; apps usually do not.
  • Does exec-form CMD fix it automatically? -> It makes the app PID 1, but the app still needs a SIGTERM handler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue consumer lost messages on every deploy for months because start.sh swallowed SIGTERM; the fix was the single word exec.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the grace period.
  • Hire: identifies PID 1 signal handling and uses exec form.
  • Strong hire: covers zombies, tini, preStop, exit code 137 meaning, and a test for graceful shutdown.

questions.promptHtml: How do Kubernetes CPU and memory requests and limits map onto cgroups, and what happens at the limit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many engineers treat requests as enforced and limits as soft. It exposes whether you know what the kernel actually does.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Requests are for scheduling and, for CPU, a relative weight (cpu.weight) that only matters under contention; limits are hard caps. A CPU limit becomes a quota in cpu.max; hitting it throttles all threads until the next period. A memory limit is memory.max; hitting it after reclaim fails gets the process OOM-killed with SIGKILL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two styles of limit:

  • Weights (shares): cpu.weight 200 vs 100 gives 2:1 only when both are busy; idle CPU is free for anyone.
  • Hard caps: cpu.max = 100000 100000 (1 CPU) and memory.max always enforced.
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduling + cpu.weight
  limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "512Mi" }   # cpu.max = 100000 100000, memory.max=512Mi
$ cd /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-3f9a....scope
$ cat memory.max cpu.max pids.max
536870912
150000 100000     # 150 ms quota per 100 ms = 1.5 CPUs
max

QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable, BestEffort. Under node memory pressure BestEffort is evicted first; oom_score_adj is -997 for Guaranteed and 1000 for BestEffort. cgroup v1 used memory.limit_in_bytes; v2 (unified, default in current distros, Kubernetes 1.25+ GA support) uses memory.max.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing the CPU request guarantees a core. It is a weight plus a scheduling hint.
  • Believing the memory request is enforced at runtime. It affects placement and eviction ranking only.
  • Mixing up v1 and v2 file names.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does memory.high do? -> Throttles and reclaims aggressively before the hard max.
  2. Why set memory request = limit? -> Predictable; avoids node-level eviction from overcommit.
  3. Should every pod have a CPU limit? -> Debatable; for latency-critical services many set requests only (see throttling).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "limits are max, requests are min". Senior: weights vs caps, exact cgroup files, QoS/eviction and the consequences (throttling vs OOM kill).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A node full of Burstable pods with limits much higher than requests hit node memory pressure and evicted a neighbour's database pod.

questions.contextHtml:
CI builds take 11 minutes on every commit even for a one-line change, the final image is 1.4 GB, and a security review flags that the process runs as root. Dockerfile:

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN mvn -B package -DskipTests
EXPOSE 8080
CMD java -jar target/app.jar

The registry also shows .git and test fixtures inside the image. A red herring: the team blames the slow Maven mirror.
questions.promptHtml: List what is wrong and fix the Dockerfile.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use alpine to make it smaller." Alpine (musl) can cause DNS and perf quirks and does not fix cache invalidation or root.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have a .dockerignore? Is BuildKit on with cache mounts? Does the app need glibc? How do we debug without a shell?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a .dockerignore (.git, target, IDE files) and split dependency resolution into its own layer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) COPY . . before dependency resolution invalidates the cache on every source change, so Maven re-downloads everything; (b) single-stage build ships the JDK, Maven and sources; (c) no USER; (d) shell-form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1 and swallows SIGTERM.
  4. How I'd verify: docker history image (layer sizes), docker build output showing which step is not CACHED, docker run --rm image id.
  5. Root cause: Layers are cached by instruction and content. Anything after a changed COPY is rebuilt, so putting the volatile source before slow, stable steps defeats caching.
  6. Fix:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd -u 10001 app
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar /app.jar
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]

Image drops from about 1.4 GB to about 250 MB (verify) and incremental builds take seconds. 7. Prevention: Hadolint in CI, image scanning, a size budget check, and non-root enforced by Pod Security admission. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Distroless gives smaller attack surface but no shell; I would pair it with kubectl debug ephemeral containers. I would not use latest tags or bake secrets into layers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Secret needed at build time? -> BuildKit --mount=type=secret, never COPY or ARG (they stay in layers).
  • Why does image digest matter? -> Tags are mutable; pin by digest for reproducibility.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A leaked credentials file was found in an old layer of a base image; deleting it in a later RUN rm did not remove it from the earlier layer.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only suggests a smaller base image.
  • Hire: fixes cache order, multi-stage, non-root.
  • Strong hire: also exec-form entrypoint, .dockerignore, cache mounts, secrets in layers and debuggability trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: How do image layers and overlayfs work, and why is writing heavily inside a container slow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of copy-on-write storage and why state belongs in volumes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An image is a stack of read-only layers, each a tarball of file changes identified by a SHA-256 digest. overlayfs merges them: lower dirs are read-only layers, the upper dir is the container's writable layer, merged is what the process sees. Writing to a file from a lower layer triggers copy-up: the whole file is copied into the upper layer first. Heavy writes are slow and vanish with the container, so data goes on volumes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ docker inspect web --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.MergedDir}}'
/var/lib/docker/overlay2/9c1a.../merged
$ mount | grep overlay
overlay on .../merged type overlay (rw,lowerdir=l/AA:l/BB:l/CC,upperdir=9c1a.../diff,workdir=9c1a.../work)
  • Reads: found in the highest layer that has the file.
  • Delete: creates a "whiteout" file in the upper layer; the lower copy remains in the image (why deleting a secret in a later layer does not remove it).
  • Copy-up: modifying a 500 MB log file in a lower layer copies all 500 MB first.
  • Volumes and bind mounts bypass overlayfs and run at native filesystem speed.

Layer order controls build cache reuse: stable steps first (OS packages, dependency install), volatile source last. Multi-stage builds keep compilers out of the final image.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing a database in the container layer and losing it on redeploy.
  • Believing rm in a later layer shrinks the image.
  • Running write-heavy workloads (databases, logs) on overlayfs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do two images share disk space? -> Identical layers (same digest) are stored once.
  2. What is a bind mount vs a named volume? -> Bind mount maps a host path; named volume is managed by Docker, both bypass overlay.
  3. Why can a pod hit DiskPressure? -> Container logs and writable layers fill the node; use ephemeral-storage limits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "layers cache builds". Senior: copy-up, whiteouts, secret leakage, volumes for state and node disk pressure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service writing a 2 GB temp file on the container layer slowed 5x and filled the node's disk, evicting neighbours.

questions.contextHtml:
An API pod has requests.cpu: 1, limits.cpu: 1, runs 8 worker threads and normally serves 500 rps. p99 jumped from 40 ms to 280 ms after a deploy, but the dashboards look healthy:

kubectl top pod api-7d9f      CPU: 310m / 1000m      Memory: 410Mi
node CPU:                    22%
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat
nr_periods     612300
nr_throttled   301220
throttled_usec 4812001299

Red herring: heap and GC logs look normal.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU is only 31%, so it is not CPU." Averages hide the throttle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the deploy raise thread counts or add parallel work (for example new startup warmers, parallel streams)? Is the JVM/Go runtime aware of the quota? What is the node's core count?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the CPU limit (for example 4) or remove it, keeping the request; roll out and watch p99.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bursty multi-threaded work burns the 100 ms quota in a few ms and all threads are frozen; (b) the runtime sized pools by host cores; (c) old kernel accounting bug (fixed in 5.4).
  4. How I'd verify: nr_throttled / nr_periods = 49% of periods throttled; throttled_usec about 4,812 s total; Prometheus rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]).
  5. Root cause: limits.cpu: 1 is 100 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, shared by all threads. Eight busy threads exhaust it in 12.5 ms and then everything is paused for the remaining 87.5 ms, even though the machine is idle. A 20 ms request can wait up to 87.5 ms more.
  6. Fix: Short term: raise or remove the limit. Long term: size thread pools to the quota (-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2, GOMAXPROCS via automaxprocs), consider static CPU manager (exclusive cores) for Guaranteed pods, or cgroup v2 cpu.max.burst (kernel 5.14+).
  7. Prevention: Alert on throttle ratio above 5 to 10%; dashboards of throttled seconds next to latency; load test with the real limit.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dropping limits trades fairness for latency, so keep requests accurate and a memory limit always. I would not trust kubectl top averages.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does a liveness probe sometimes fail in this state? -> The probe thread is frozen with the rest; raise timeoutSeconds or fix the throttle.
  • Does adding replicas help? -> It reduces per-pod burst, but the root cause remains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A batch of 64-core nodes ran a service with a 1 CPU limit and 64 GC threads. Latency spikes disappeared only after ActiveProcessorCount was set.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reads averages and looks at GC.
  • Hire: checks cpu.stat, explains quota per period.
  • Strong hire: ties thread counts to quota, discusses limit removal, burst, cpuset, and alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java 21 service has limits.memory: 1Gi and starts with -Xmx1g. Every few hours the pod restarts. kubectl get pod shows RESTARTS climbing; heap dumps and app logs show no OutOfMemoryError.

$ kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -A4 'Last State'
    Last State:   Terminated
      Reason:     OOMKilled
      Exit Code:  137
$ dmesg -T | grep -i killed
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18211 (java) anon-rss:1048200kB file-rss:12288kB
JVM metrics: heap used 900 MiB, threads 210, direct buffers 150 MiB

Red herring: someone suspects a memory leak in business code.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it dying and how do you size it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the memory limit" without explaining that Xmx equal to the limit guarantees the kill.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the baseline vs peak RSS? Is heap usage a sawtooth or a ramp? Any emptyDir in memory? How many threads and Netty direct buffers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the limit to 1.5Gi and set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 in place of -Xmx.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) non-heap memory (metaspace, 210 thread stacks x 1 MiB, code cache, direct buffers, GC structures) plus a full heap exceeds the cgroup limit; (b) real leak (check trend); (c) tmpfs or page cache counting against the cgroup.
  4. How I'd verify: NMT (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, jcmd VM.native_memory), memory.stat (anon vs file), memory.events oom_kill, RSS graph over time.
  5. Root cause: memory.max covers heap plus everything else. 900 MiB heap + about 90 MiB metaspace + 210 MiB stacks + 150 MiB direct = about 1.35 GiB, so under load the kernel finds nothing to reclaim and SIGKILLs the JVM, exit 137, no stack trace, no chance to log.
  6. Fix: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65-70, limit 1.5Gi, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m, -Xss512k if safe, fewer threads. If the RSS is a ramp that never falls, take a heap dump and use NMT to find the leak.
  7. Prevention: Alert on working-set / limit above 85%; dashboards separating heap, non-heap, RSS; load test with production-like concurrency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set the limit very high "just in case" since packing density and node pressure suffer. I would not enable swap to hide the problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same issue in Go or Node? -> Go: GOMEMLIMIT at about 90% of the limit; Node: --max-old-space-size below the limit.
  • Why do glibc arenas inflate RSS? -> Per-thread arenas fragment; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 often helps.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A service ran fine for months until a new feature added 300 threads; the extra 300 MiB of stacks was exactly what pushed it past its limit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: assumes a code leak; raises Xmx.
  • Hire: explains non-heap memory and sets a percentage.
  • Strong hire: NMT, cgroup stats, exit 137 meaning, alerts on working set, runtime-specific flags.

questions.promptHtml: Why can a container with a 1-CPU limit running on a 64-core node behave badly, and what do you do about the runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the interaction between kernel quota, runtimes that read core counts, and thread pool sizing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A CPU limit is a time quota per 100 ms period, not a number of cores. A runtime that sizes its thread pools by the visible 64 cores starts 64 GC and worker threads that burn the quota in a couple of milliseconds, and then the whole group is paused until the next period. So I make the runtime quota-aware or set pool sizes explicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Limit 1 CPU = cpu.max "100000 100000" (100 ms per 100 ms).
8 busy threads: 100 ms quota is spent in 12.5 ms, then 87.5 ms frozen.
  • JVM: container-aware since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191); -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N overrides. It computes cores from the quota, but libraries (Netty, ForkJoin) may still size from it, check them.
  • Go: before Go 1.25 GOMAXPROCS saw host cores; use uber-go/automaxprocs (newer Go respects the quota, verify your version).
  • Node/Python: worker counts from os.cpus() can oversubscribe.
  • Alternatives: static CPU manager gives exclusive cores for Guaranteed pods with integer CPU; cpu.max.burst allows accumulated quota to be used (kernel 5.14+).
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat
nr_periods 612300
nr_throttled 301220      # ~49% of periods throttled

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading cpu: 1 as one core.
  • Judging health from average CPU %.
  • Not telling the runtime about the limit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Should we remove CPU limits? -> For latency-critical services many operators set requests only, with memory limit = request; keep limits where noisy-neighbour fairness matters.
  2. Metric to watch? -> Throttled periods / periods ratio.
  3. What about cpuset? -> Pins to specific cores; no quota throttling but no bursting either.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "set a CPU limit". Senior: knows quota mechanics, runtime thread sizing, and the trade-off between limits and requests-only.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Go service with 1 CPU limit on large nodes saw p99 spikes until automaxprocs was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A Go service in a distroless image (no shell, no curl) enters CrashLoopBackOff at 02:00 after a config change. On-call sees:

$ kubectl get pod
payments-6f8   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   7 (45s ago)
$ kubectl logs payments-6f8
(empty)
$ kubectl exec -it payments-6f8 -- sh
OCI runtime exec failed: exec: "sh": executable file not found
$ kubectl describe pod payments-6f8 | grep -E 'Reason|Exit|Liveness'
Reason: Error    Exit Code: 1
Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.2.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded

Red herring: the node was also upgraded the same night.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find out what is wrong with no shell and no useful logs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rebuild the image with a shell." Slow, changes the artifact, and loses the failing state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly changed (config, image, secrets)? Does it fail on all pods? Previous instance's logs? Does staging reproduce?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the config/deploy (kubectl rollout undo) to restore service, preserve the failing manifest for analysis.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bad config or missing secret causing a startup failure; (b) liveness probe killing a slow-starting app (use a startup probe); (c) resource limit (OOM would show 137, not 1); (d) node upgrade/CNI issue.
  4. How I'd verify: kubectl logs --previous (the new instance is empty, the crashed one has the output); kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp; an ephemeral container sharing the target's namespaces: kubectl debug -it payments-6f8 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=payments; from the node, crictl inspect to get the PID then nsenter -t $PID -n ss -tnp and tcpdump.
  5. Root cause: Example: the new config pointed at a secret key that did not exist, the app exited with code 1 before logging (logger not initialised); the --previous log or /proc/PID/environ via the debug container shows the missing variable. The liveness failure was a symptom of restarts.
  6. Fix: Correct the config, add startup validation that logs the reason before exit, add a startup probe so liveness does not kill a slow start.
kubectl logs payments-6f8 --previous
kubectl debug -it payments-6f8 --image=busybox --target=payments --copy-to=payments-dbg -- sh
  1. Prevention: Config schema validation in CI, startup probes, structured logging initialised first, a runbook for distroless debugging.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not permanently ship a shell in prod images; ephemeral containers keep the attack surface small. I would not exec into a node and edit files by hand.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The pod restarts every 30 s and evidence is lost? -> --copy-to a debug copy with the command overridden to sleep, or use kubectl debug node.
  • How to see the app's syscalls? -> Ephemeral container with strace and shareProcessNamespace, or strace from the node.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A crash loop turned out to be a liveness probe at 1 s timeout on a CPU-throttled app that needed 3 s to warm up; the fix was a startup probe and a larger CPU request.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rebuilds images, restarts blindly.
  • Hire: uses --previous, events, and an ephemeral debug container.
  • Strong hire: rolls back first, nsenter/crictl from the node, startup probe, and prevention.

questions.promptHtml: What are the different kinds of out-of-memory events with containers on Kubernetes, and how do you tell them apart?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The fix differs completely: a bigger limit versus fixing node packing or requests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A container OOM happens inside one cgroup: the container hit its own memory.max, the cgroup OOM killer SIGKILLs a process, exit code 137 and Kubernetes shows OOMKilled; only that container dies. A node-level event is the host being out of memory: the kubelet evicts pods by QoS (Evicted, BestEffort first) or, if it is too slow, the global kernel OOM killer picks victims by oom_score. The first is a sizing problem for one workload, the second a node-packing and requests problem.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ kubectl describe pod api | grep -A5 'Last State'
   Reason: OOMKilled   Exit Code: 137          # cgroup OOM
$ dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18211 (java) ...   # "Memory cgroup" = container
Out of memory: Killed process ...                              # no "cgroup" = global OOM
$ cat memory.events
oom_kill 3

What counts toward the limit: anon memory (heap, stacks), page cache (reclaimable first), tmpfs and emptyDir: medium: Memory, kernel memory. Kubernetes evicts on the working set (container_memory_working_set_bytes, usage minus inactive file cache). oom_score_adj: Guaranteed -997, BestEffort 1000, Burstable in between (scaled by request).

usage hits memory.max -> reclaim page cache/swap -> nothing left -> cgroup OOM kill (SIGKILL)
node low on memory   -> kubelet evicts by QoS     -> else kernel global OOM killer

Swap was traditionally disabled on nodes; cgroup v2 memory.swap.max and NodeSwap exist now (check version).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debugging exit 137 as an app crash.
  • Thinking page cache is free: it counts, though it is reclaimed first.
  • Ignoring sidecars (Envoy) with small limits, and memory-backed emptyDir.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which pod dies first on node pressure? -> BestEffort, then Burstable exceeding requests, Guaranteed last.
  2. Why set memory limit = request? -> Predictable behaviour and no overcommit-driven evictions.
  3. How to tell a leak from a low limit? -> Ramp that never falls vs a sawtooth to a baseline.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "OOMKilled means raise memory". Senior: distinguishes cgroup from global OOM, QoS ordering, working-set metric, and runtime flags.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tmpfs emptyDir used as a scratch directory counted against the container and caused OOMKills that looked like heap problems.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem draft: "At 11:20 a traffic burst (2x) caused 40% of pods in the checkout deployment to restart within 3 minutes, which reduced capacity and caused a full outage for 14 minutes." Facts:

liveness: httpGet /healthz  timeoutSeconds: 1  periodSeconds: 5  failureThreshold: 3
resources: requests.cpu 500m  limits.cpu 500m   (JVM, 8 threads)
Events: "Liveness probe failed: context deadline exceeded" x3 -> "Killing container"
cpu.stat: throttled in ~70% of periods during the incident
No OOMKilled, exit code 143

Autoscaler HPA target is 70% average CPU; HPA reacted 4 minutes after the burst.
questions.promptHtml: Write the root cause analysis and the action items.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Traffic spike caused the outage; add more pods." Misses that the health probe amplified the failure into a cascade.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was /healthz on the same thread pool as user traffic? Did restarted pods need a long warm-up? What did the HPA metric show (throttled CPU hides demand)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (during incident) Remove or loosen the liveness probe, manually scale up, shed load; avoid mass-restarting.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CPU throttling froze threads so /healthz missed 1 s three times; (b) restarting pods cold started with JIT warmup, taking more CPU, and more throttling; (c) HPA lagged because throttled CPU usage stays at the limit (looks like 70% of 500m) and the metric window is long.
  4. How I'd verify: Throttle ratio on cadvisor metrics, probe logs, the event timeline, HPA decisions, JIT/startup CPU.
  5. Root cause: A cascade: burst leads to quota exhaustion, which freezes all threads including health handlers, liveness fails, kubelet kills healthy-but-slow pods, which reduces capacity, which raises load on survivors. The root cause is liveness probing a component that is only slow, plus limits too tight for a multi-threaded runtime.
  6. Fix: Liveness should only detect a dead process (cheap, separate endpoint/thread); use readiness for "temporarily busy"; add a startup probe; timeoutSeconds 3 to 5; raise or remove the CPU limit; thread counts matched to quota; HPA on request rate or latency plus a lower CPU target and faster scale-up behaviour.
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }, timeoutSeconds: 3, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 6 }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }, timeoutSeconds: 2, periodSeconds: 5 }
startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 2 }
  1. Prevention: Load test the 2x burst; alert on throttle ratio and restart counts; chaos test with CPU contention; runbook entry for "do not restart on overload".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not disable liveness completely, since real deadlocks exist; I would keep it cheap and conservative.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why exit 143? -> SIGTERM (128 + 15) from the kubelet killing on probe failure, unlike 137 (SIGKILL/OOM).
  • Should readiness share the same endpoint? -> Separate: liveness answers "is the process wedged", readiness answers "should I get traffic".

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet-wide restart loop was triggered by a database slowdown because the liveness endpoint called the database. Pods were killed for a dependency's fault.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames traffic and asks for more pods.
  • Hire: identifies throttling and liveness cascade, fixes probes.
  • Strong hire: separates liveness/readiness/startup, HPA behaviour, evidence-based timeline, concrete action items with owners.

questions.contextHtml: You are building a "run your own code" feature for customers (a CI-like service). Today an engineer proposes: every job runs in a Docker container started by the API server, which mounts /var/run/docker.sock to start siblings; containers run as root with --privileged so jobs can build Docker images; all jobs share one node pool with other internal services. Expected load: 5,000 jobs/hour, jobs up to 30 min, some from free-tier anonymous users.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with this design, and what would you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Docker is isolated enough." Containers share the host kernel, and --privileged plus the socket is effectively root on the node.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the code trusted (employees) or hostile (anonymous users)? Do jobs need Docker-in-Docker? What data lives on the same nodes? What are compliance requirements?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop mounting the socket and drop --privileged; run as non-root with --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --read-only; move anonymous jobs off shared nodes.
  3. Hypotheses (risks), ranked: (a) socket or privileged mode gives host root, so any job escapes to other tenants' data and internal services; (b) shared kernel: one kernel CVE crosses tenants; (c) resource abuse: crypto-mining, fork bombs; (d) network access to internal metadata services.
  4. How I'd verify: Pen test: from a job run docker ps, mount the host root, read the cloud metadata endpoint; audit seccomp/capabilities with docker inspect; check cgroup limits exist.
  5. Root cause: The design treats a container as a security boundary equal to a VM. Namespaces hide, they do not defend; the kernel is shared.
  6. Fix: For hostile code use VM-grade isolation: Firecracker/Kata microVMs or gVisor, one sandbox per job, ephemeral, destroyed afterwards. Dedicated node pool with no internal secrets, egress firewall blocking metadata and internal ranges, user namespaces/rootless, seccomp, pids.max, memory and CPU limits, disk quotas, timeouts. For image builds use rootless BuildKit or Kaniko in a sandbox rather than privileged DinD.
  7. Prevention: Threat model review, automated escape tests in CI, audit logging, quotas per tenant.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: MicroVMs cost more start time (about 100 to 200 ms for Firecracker, verify) and density but buy safety; plain containers are fine for trusted internal jobs. I would not build my own sandbox.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How does gVisor differ from Kata? -> gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel; Kata runs a lightweight VM with its own kernel.
  • What does user namespaces buy? -> Even if a process escapes, it is an unprivileged host UID.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A CI platform mounted the Docker socket; a customer job listed every other tenant's containers and read their environment variables, including cloud keys.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: considers the design fine or only drops root.
  • Hire: removes socket/privileged, adds limits and capabilities, proposes stronger isolation.
  • Strong hire: threat model driven; microVMs/gVisor with cost trade-offs; network egress controls; rootless builds.

questions.contextHtml:
A pod in Kubernetes intermittently shows 5-second delays on outbound calls to internal services; at other times the pod throws fork: Resource temporarily unavailable and Too many open files. Facts:

$ kubectl exec app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.96.0.10   search ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local   options ndots:5
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../pids.current /sys/fs/cgroup/.../pids.max
4093
4096
$ nsenter -t $PID -n ss -s
estab 12, timewait 3
$ nstat -az | grep -i insert_failed
IpExtInInsertFailed ... conntrack insert_failed 18433

Red herring: CPU and memory are comfortable.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms and how you would investigate from the node.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It is DNS, restart CoreDNS" and "raise ulimit" without finding who is leaking threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do delays happen at exactly 5 s (the resolver timeout)? Which workload creates threads (a bug that spawns per request)? Is it only some nodes (conntrack tables)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart leaking pods one at a time behind readiness; enable NodeLocal DNSCache; temporarily raise pids.max.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pids leak: thread-per-request without cap or unreaped children, reaching pids.max 4096; (b) DNS: parallel A/AAAA queries race in conntrack (insert_failed), the lost packet is retried after 5 s; ndots:5 multiplies lookups; (c) fd leak.
  4. How I'd verify: cat pids.current trend, ls /proc/$PID/task | wc -l, jstack/pstack grouped by name; from the node nsenter -t $PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 port 53 to see duplicate queries and the 5 s gap; conntrack -S for insert_failed; lsof -p/ls /proc/$PID/fd | wc -l against /proc/$PID/limits.
  5. Root cause: Two independent problems. A thread leak hits the cgroup pids cap so fork/clone returns EAGAIN. Separately, DNS UDP queries over the same 5-tuple race in conntrack on older kernels, one gets dropped, and glibc waits 5 s before retry; ndots:5 makes each external name try several search domains first.
  6. Fix: Fix the thread leak (bounded pools, reap children, use tini); set pids.max with headroom and alerts. For DNS: NodeLocal DNSCache, use FQDNs with a trailing dot or lower ndots to 2 in dnsConfig, single-request-reopen, or upgrade to a kernel that fixes the race; raise nf_conntrack_max.
dnsConfig: { options: [ { name: ndots, value: "2" } ] }
  1. Prevention: Alerts on pids.current / pids.max, conntrack insert_failed, DNS latency; runbook that includes nsenter recipes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blindly set pids.max to unlimited: a fork bomb would then hurt the node. Not disable conntrack without understanding NAT dependencies.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why 5 seconds exactly? -> The default resolver timeout of glibc; a single dropped UDP packet costs one full timeout.
  • Why does Too many open files appear with pids limits? -> Same leak pattern also leaks fds; limits are separate (nofile vs pids.max).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet-wide 5 s latency tail disappeared the day NodeLocal DNSCache was rolled out, and nobody had touched the application.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts things; raises limits without diagnosis.
  • Hire: separates the two problems; uses cgroup pids and DNS analysis.
  • Strong hire: nsenter + tcpdump + conntrack evidence, ndots, NodeLocal DNS, leak fix and monitoring.
